lead: This unit turns a set of linear equations into a matrix, reduces the matrix by safe row moves, and reads off whether a solution exists and how many. After it you can solve small and medium systems by hand with Gaussian or Gauss–Jordan elimination, state the rank test for consistency, and factor a matrix as A = LU where that is allowed.
about: Chapter 1.1 writes a system of linear equations as a matrix equation Ax = b and separates the homogeneous case from the non-homogeneous one. Chapter 1.2 introduces the three elementary row operations and the staircase forms they produce. Chapter 1.3 turns those operations into two named algorithms, Gaussian elimination with back substitution and Gauss–Jordan elimination. Chapter 1.4 uses the pivot count to define rank and gives the rank test for consistency and for the number of solutions. Chapter 1.5, taught in only a few universities, records the same elimination as a product A = LU so that repeated solves become two triangular solves.

chapters.idea: A linear system is a set of straight-line constraints, and writing it as Ax = b separates the coefficients from the right-hand side so the pattern of solutions becomes visible.
chapters.depth: Matrix form: A is the m×n coefficient matrix (m equations, n unknowns), x is the column of unknowns, b is the right-hand side column. Define homogeneous (b = 0) and non-homogeneous (b ≠ 0). The homogeneous system always has the trivial solution x = 0; the real question is whether other solutions exist. Show the three outcomes for two unknowns: one point (lines meet), no point (parallel lines), a whole line (coincident lines). Introduce the augmented matrix [A|b] and say it carries all the information. A system with at least one solution is consistent, one with none is inconsistent; introduce both words here.

figure.title: From a problem to an augmented matrix
figure.aria: A left-to-right flow from a word problem to linear equations, then to the matrix form Ax = b, then to the augmented matrix [A|b].

chapters.example: Write the system x + y + z = 6, x − y + 2z = 5, 2x + y − z = 1 as Ax = b and form the augmented matrix; then verify that x = 1, y = 2, z = 3 is a solution. Here A = [[1,1,1],[1,−1,2],[2,1,−1]] and b = (6,5,1). Check: 1 + 2 + 3 = 6; 1 − 2 + 6 = 5; 2 + 2 − 3 = 1.
chapters.trap: Assuming every homogeneous system has only x = 0. The trivial solution always exists; extra solutions depend on the coefficients. Also, a row operation must act on the whole augmented row, including the b column.
chapters.leave: Rank and the count of solutions go to 1.4; elimination steps to 1.2 and 1.3; the vector-space view of the solution set to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: Three reversible row moves change a matrix's appearance but not its solution set, and repeating them produces a staircase form that is easy to read.
chapters.depth: The three elementary row operations: swap two rows (Ri ↔ Rj); multiply a row by a nonzero scalar k (kRi); add a multiple of one row to another (Ri + kRj). Explain why each is reversible, so the solution set is unchanged. Define pivot (first nonzero entry of a row) and row equivalence. Echelon form: nonzero rows above zero rows, each pivot to the right of the pivot above, zeros below every pivot. Reduced row echelon form (RREF): every pivot is 1 and is the only nonzero entry in its column. Some syllabi call RREF the row canonical form or the fully reduced normal form. Echelon form is not unique; RREF is.

figure.title: Row operations to reduced form
figure.aria: A top-to-bottom flow from the augmented matrix through pivot choice and clearing below to echelon form, then clearing above to the reduced form.

chapters.example: Reduce the augmented matrix of x + 2y + z = 4, 2x + 5y + 3z = 9, x + 3y + 3z = 6 to echelon form, then to reduced echelon form. Start [[1,2,1,4],[2,5,3,9],[1,3,3,6]]. R2 − 2R1 gives [0,1,1,1]; R3 − R1 gives [0,1,2,2]; R3 − R2 gives [0,0,1,1]. Echelon form: [[1,2,1,4],[0,1,1,1],[0,0,1,1]]. Then R2 − R3 gives [0,1,0,0]; R1 − R3 gives [1,2,0,3]; R1 − 2R2 gives [1,0,0,3]. So x = 3, y = 0, z = 1; check: 3 + 0 + 1 = 4, 6 + 0 + 3 = 9, 3 + 0 + 3 = 6.
chapters.trap: Scaling a row by zero (not allowed), or forgetting that the augmented column changes too. A common exam error is treating echelon form as unique and comparing two different correct echelon forms.
chapters.leave: Pivot counting for rank to 1.4; the full algorithm to 1.3; recording multipliers for LU to 1.5.

chapters.idea: Elimination is a recipe: push zeros under the pivots, then either substitute upward or push zeros above the pivots too, and read the answer.
chapters.depth: Gaussian elimination: forward elimination to echelon form, then back substitution from the last pivot upward. Gauss–Jordan: continue until reduced echelon form; no back substitution, the solution is read directly. Write the pivot, the multiplier and the update rule step by step. If a pivot is 0, swap with a lower row; if the whole pivot column below is zero, skip it and that unknown becomes free. Count: with r pivots and n unknowns there are n − r free parameters; write the general solution with parameters. One line on partial pivoting (take the largest available pivot) for hand and computer work.

figure.aria: A decision tree: from the row reduction of the augmented matrix, one branch stops at echelon form and back-substitutes, the other continues to reduced form and reads the solution directly.

chapters.example: Solve x + y + z = 3, 2x + 2y + 2z = 6, x − y = 0 by Gaussian elimination and give the general solution. Augmented matrix: [[1,1,1,3],[2,2,2,6],[1,−1,0,0]]. R2 − 2R1 gives the zero row [0,0,0,0]. R3 − R1 gives [0,−2,−1,−3]. Move the zero row to the bottom and scale the other row by −1/2: [[1,1,1,3],[0,1,1/2,3/2],[0,0,0,0]]. Put z = t. Then y = (3 − t)/2 and x = 3 − y − z = (3 − t)/2. General solution: x = (3 − t)/2, y = (3 − t)/2, z = t; at t = 1 this gives (1,1,1), which checks in all three equations.
chapters.trap: Dividing by a zero pivot without swapping rows; losing a free variable by treating a skipped column as a pivot column.
chapters.leave: Why row operations preserve the solution set to 1.2; rank and consistency tests to 1.4; operation counts and numerical stability to a numerical methods course.

chapters.idea: Rank counts the pivots, and three numbers (rank A, rank [A|b], and n) decide whether the system has no solution, one solution, or infinitely many.
chapters.depth: Rank of A: the number of nonzero rows in any echelon form, equivalently the number of pivots; state that row rank equals column rank. Consistency test: if rank(A) < rank([A|b]) the system is inconsistent; if rank(A) = rank([A|b]) = n there is a unique solution; if rank(A) = rank([A|b]) = r < n there are infinitely many, with n − r free variables. Homogeneous case: always consistent, nonzero solutions exactly when r < n, and the solution set has dimension n − r (its nullity). Mention that some syllabi define rank as the order of the largest non-vanishing minor and connect the two views. Sketch, do not fully prove, row rank = column rank.

figure.aria: A decision tree that compares the rank of the coefficient matrix with the rank of the augmented matrix and then with the number of unknowns, ending in no solution, a unique solution, or n minus r free variables.

chapters.example: Decide the nature of the solutions and solve: x + 2y + 3z = 4, 2x + 4y + 6z = 8, x + y + z = 3. The second row is twice the first, so it adds no pivot. R3 − R1 gives [0,−1,−2,−1], a pivot. Hence rank A = 2 and rank [A|b] = 2, while n = 3, so there are infinitely many solutions with n − r = 1 free variable. From y + 2z = 1 we get y = 1 − 2z; then x = 3 − y − z = 2 + z. With z = t: (x, y, z) = (2 + t, 1 − 2t, t). Check at t = 1, (3,−1,1): 3 − 2 + 3 = 4, 6 − 4 + 6 = 8, 3 − 1 + 1 = 3.
chapters.trap: Checking only rank(A) = rank([A|b]) and declaring a unique solution; or thinking rank(A) < n alone gives infinitely many solutions, when the augmented rank must match first.
chapters.leave: Null space, column space and the rank-nullity theorem as subspace statements to Units 2 and 3; determinant-based rank to Unit 4 if determinants are listed there.

chapters.idea: Gaussian elimination can be written as a product A = LU, after which solving Ax = b costs two triangular solves instead of a fresh elimination.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. L is unit lower triangular (1s on the diagonal, multipliers below it), U is upper triangular (the echelon form). Doolittle form as above; mention that Crout form puts the pivots in L. Existence: no row swap is needed when every leading principal minor of A is nonzero; otherwise PA = LU with a permutation matrix P. Algorithm: for each column k, store the multiplier ℓik = aik/akk and subtract ℓik times row k. Solve Ly = b from the top, then Ux = y from the bottom. One line on cost: about 2n³/3 operations for the factorization, reused for every new b.

figure.title: One factorization, two triangular solves
figure.aria: A left-to-right flow: Ax = b is factored as A = LU, then Ly = b is solved forward, Ux = y is solved backward, and x comes out.

chapters.example: Factor A = [[2,1,1],[4,3,3],[8,7,9]] as A = LU, then solve Ax = b for b = (4,10,24). Elimination: multiplier 2 on row 2 and 4 on row 3 remove column 1, giving rows [0,1,1] and [0,3,5]; multiplier 3 on row 3 removes column 2, giving [0,0,2]. So L = [[1,0,0],[2,1,0],[4,3,1]] and U = [[2,1,1],[0,1,1],[0,0,2]]. Solve Ly = b: y1 = 4, 2(4) + y2 = 10 gives y2 = 2, 4(4) + 3(2) + y3 = 24 gives y3 = 2. Solve Ux = y: 2x3 = 2 gives x3 = 1; x2 + x3 = 2 gives x2 = 1; 2x1 + x2 + x3 = 4 gives x1 = 1. Answer x = (1,1,1).
chapters.trap: Putting the multipliers into U instead of L; assuming every square matrix has an LU factorization with no row swaps.
chapters.leave: Pivoting and PLU in detail, and Cholesky factorization, to a numerical methods course; QR and SVD to Unit 5.
